# Supplier Partnership Strategy for CBAM: Steel & Aluminum from India, Turkey, and North Africa (2026–2030)

*A decision-ready framework for converting a regulatory shock into a co-built capability — preserving supply relationships and shared competitiveness despite divergent perceptions of fairness.*

---

## Core Principle

CBAM transforms every imported tonne into two products: the metal, and the **verified carbon data attached to it**. The reflex response — pushing reporting burden and certificate costs down onto suppliers — converts a regulatory event into a relationship rupture, especially where CBAM is read as disguised protectionism. The alternative: treat compliance as a **co-built capability** and carbon intensity as a **shared commercial variable**.

The architecture is two-layered:

- **Layer 1 — Compliance Core (non-negotiable, centrally owned):** verified actual embedded-emissions data to EU methodology, installation-level monitoring plans, accredited third-party verification, contractually guaranteed data delivery, zero reliance on default values. Identical for every supplier — because Brussels accepts no excuses, the buyer can accept no exceptions.
- **Layer 2 — Partnership Layer (differentiated by archetype and country):** framing, financing, technical support, advocacy, pacing. Radically different by supplier.

**The grievance and the gap are the same problem.** A supplier who believes CBAM is protectionism will comply minimally and invest nothing; a supplier who sees the buyer sharing cost and advocating on its behalf will compete for you in a decarbonizing market. Perception management is not soft diplomacy — it is the mechanism that determines data quality, and data quality determines cost.

---

## 1. The Strategic Read

**The cost curve creates a window.** With the CBAM factor mirroring the EU ETS free-allocation phase-out, financial exposure starts small and steepens:

| Year | CBAM factor | Illustrative cost/t (BF-BOF steel at ~2.3 tCO₂/t, EUA at €80) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026 | 2.5% | ~€5 |
| 2028 | 10% | ~€18 |
| 2030 | 48.5% | ~€89 |
| 2034 | 100% | ~€184 |

2026–2028 are the **cheap years** — the time to build data capability and abatement pipelines before the curve bites. Suppliers who treat 2026's modest cost as the steady state are miscalibrated; suppliers who see the 2030 number understand why this is strategic.

**Data failure is a direct cost.** Where actual verified data is absent, punitive default values apply, with mark-ups over time. This converts supplier capability into buyer P&L — the argument for funding capability rather than demanding it.

**Scope risk favors early movers.** Steel and aluminum currently face direct-emissions accounting; indirect (electricity) emissions are under review. Since electricity is ~60–70% of aluminum's footprint and the Turkish EAF advantage rests partly on grid assumptions, renewable PPAs now are both hedge and competitiveness play.

---

## 2. Supplier Archetypes

Segment on two axes — technical readiness and posture — because the same mill can be capable and resentful, or willing

run.userPrompt:
With the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism entering its full financial phase in 2026, a European industrial buyer depends on steel and aluminum suppliers in India, Turkey, and North Africa that now face costly emissions reporting and carbon pricing. The suppliers vary in technical readiness and in how they perceive the mechanism, with some viewing it as disguised protectionism, straining long-standing commercial relationships.

Propose a partnership strategy for supporting emerging-market suppliers through carbon border compliance, preserving supply relationships and shared competitiveness despite differing perceptions of fairness.
